subject: How to reference variables in plyr by number or with a string

messages.author: 3a71f645a046e485
messages.subject: How to reference variables in plyr by number or with a string
parts:
Hello, I have a dataframe with some columns named itemn, where n=1 to N. I want to do some simple aggregation by groups on these columns in sequence. This is what I tried:

for(k in 1:num.items) {
   mean.score <- ddply(all.people.ok, "measure.strata", summarize, mean.score=mean(as.name(eval(paste("item", k, sep='')))))
}

But I keep getting warnings() saying
1: In mean.default(as.name(eval(paste("item", k, sep = "")))) :
  argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA

I know these are columns 17+k, but when I try

mean.score <- ddply(all.people.ok, "measure.strata", summarize, mean.score=mean(all.people.ok[, 17+k]))

it gives me  2.469589 for the value for all groups, which is the overall mean.

If someone can give me a clue on how to do this I'd be very grateful.

Even if that code succeeded, you would still have been overwriting all of the 1:(numitems-1) results. Nothing to do with plyr, of course.

Wouldn't it be easier to just use aggregate:

aggregate( all.people.ok[ , grep("item", names( all.people.ok)) ] , # item_n columns
"measure.strata", # grouping variable
FUN=mean)


(It took me an unreasonable long number of months to learn that this was exactly the purpose for `aggregate`.)

> aggregate( iris[ , grep("Sepal", names( iris)) ] , # item_n columns
+ iris["Species"], # grouping variable
+ FUN=mean)
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width
1 setosa 5.006 3.428
2 versicolor 5.936 2.770
3 virginica 6.588 2.974

I had a fair amount of trouble figuring out that this worked cleanly.

> mean.score <- ddply(iris[ , c("Species", grep("Sepal", names( iris), value=TRUE)) ]
+ , .(Species),
+ colwise(mean) )
> mean.score
Species Sepal.Length Sepal.Width
1 setosa 5.006 3.428
2 versicolor 5.936 2.770
3 virginica 6.588 2.974

Anyone who wants to "debug my brain" is welcome to the long list of failed efforts at getting plyr-functions to do this. Just send me an email.

I think help(ddply) should have a link to both the help(summarise) and the help(colwise) pages, especially now that mean.data.frame has been deprecated.

I was also able to get success with these alternates (following examples in the help page) albeit with ugly warnings:

Hi:

Is this what you had in mind?

u <- matrix(rnorm(100), nrow = 10, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("y", 1:10)))
v <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:3], c(3, 4, 3))), as.data.frame(u))
library(plyr)

# select the variables to be summarized
vnames <- paste0("y", 1:10)
# use colwise() to apply the mean function to 
# each variable in vnames
ddply(v, .(gp), colwise(mean, vnames))

HTH,

On Wednesday, October 31, 2012 11:42:08 AM UTC-5, Hadley Wickham wrote:

Ah, colwise. I was not aware of that. However, I have another idea on how to do this that should be much cleaner and more efficient. I'm going to melt those columns and then do ddply grouping by both the item and the measure.strata. Doesn't that sound better? 


Yes ;)

Here's what I did. It works waaayyy better. I do the melt'ing and ddply'ing once on the full dataframe, and then inside the for() loop, extract the data that I need. 

people.melt <- melt(all.people.ok[,  18:(17+number.items+3)], id.vars=c("compare.1", "compare.2", "measure.strata"))
people.ply <- ddply(people.melt, .(compare.1, compare.2, measure.strata, variable), summarize, mean.score=mean(value, na.rm=T))

for (k in 1:number.items) {
...
mean.score.compare.1 <- subset(people.ply, people.ply$compare.1==T & people.ply$variable==paste("item", k, sep=''))[, c("measure.strata", "mean.score")]
mean.score.compare.2 <- subset(people.ply, people.ply$compare.2==T & people.ply$variable==paste("item", k, sep=''))[, c("measure.strata", "mean.score")]
...

}

 
If for some reason you want your original approach to work, you just need to remove the as.name.

for(k in 1:num.items) {
   mean.score <- ddply(all.people.ok, "measure.strata", summarize, mean.score=mean(eval(paste("item", k, sep=''))))
}

Hmm. I thought I tried that but...
 
Thanks, Hadley.
